title: First Right-to-Work Laws Passed: Arkansas and Florida Lead Corporate Anti-Union Campaign
description: Arkansas and Florida become the first states to pass right-to-work laws in 1944, following campaigns by Vance Muse's Christian American Association, founded in 1936 with backing from Southern oil companies and Northeastern industrialists. Muse, a lobbyist for conservative and corporate interests, originated the 'right-to-work' slogan working with Dallas Morning News editorial writer William Ruggles (who suggested the name on Labor Day 1941). The Christian American Association, described by Dartmouth sociologist Marc Dixon as 'the first in the nation to champion the Right-to-Work as a full-blown political slogan,' campaigns by equating union growth with race-mixing and communism. In Arkansas, men connected to the State Chamber of Commerce/Associated Industries of Arkansas, Arkansas Expenditure Council, and Arkansas Farm Bureau Federation create the Arkansas Free Enterprise Association (AFEA) in 1946 to defend the right-to-work amendment. By 1947, 14 states have passed such legislation. The campaigns demonstrate sophisticated corporate coordination across state lines and effective use of racist and anti-communist messaging to undermine labor organizing, predating the Powell Memo by 27 years.

sources.title: The Racist Roots of 'Right to Work' Laws
Right to Work Laws: Legislative Background and Empirical Research

significance: Establishes state-level strategy for weakening unions that later becomes national template after Taft-Hartley Act (1947) authorizes right-to-work laws. Corporate backing from oil companies and industrialists demonstrates cross-industry coordination. Use of racist messaging (equating unions with race-mixing) shows willingness to exploit racial tensions to advance anti-labor agenda. The creation of state business associations (like AFEA) to lobby legislators creates replicable model used across the South. By 1950, 12 states have right-to-work laws; by 1960, 18 states—demonstrating effectiveness of corporate state-level organizing.
